title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E449 gives a residue-theoretic route to Fermat's two-squares theorem for primes p = 4n+1. The previous page established that −1 is a quadratic residue mod p, so the set of quadratic residues is closed under negation (§58).

Theorem §60, finished on this page. For any b coprime to p there is an x with x² ≡ −b² (mod p). Hence p divides b² + x². Neither b² nor x² is divisible by p, so both are prime to p.

Cor. 1 (§61). The square (mp ± x)² is congruent to x² mod p for every m. So x may be chosen with 0 < x < p/2, i.e. x ≤ 2n.

Cor. 2 (§62). Each a in {1, …, 2n} therefore has a partner b in {1, …, 2n} with p | a² + b². This gives the sequence 1+p², 4+q², 9+r², … of such sums, with all roots below 2n+1.

Cor. 3 (§63). The 2n numbers below 2n+1 are matched into pairs, and the two squares in a pair are always unequal. So there are exactly n such sums. The partners are distinct because a² ≡ −a² would force p | 2a². Uniqueness of the partner in [1, 2n] is tacit but true, since ±x are the only roots of x² ≡ c.

Since a² + b² < 2(2n+1)² = 8n² + 8n + 2, the quotient (a² + b²)/p is less than about 2n + 3/2, hence at most 2n+1.

Purpose: this yields multiples m·p = a² + b² with small m. That is the starting point for the descent argument (Euler's descent of E241 or Lagrange-style) to reach m = 1. The Scholion (§64) begins tabulating quadratic residues so that these pairs can be extracted concretely for p = 5, 13, 17, 29, 37 (next page).
errors: §63: the bound is slightly imprecise. 8n²+8n+2 divided by 4n+1 equals 2n + 3/2 + 1/(2(4n+1)), not strictly less than 2n + 3/2. Since the quotient is an integer, the conclusion (quotient ≤ 2n+1 < 2n+2) still holds.
The bound is loose in any case. With a ≠ b both ≤ 2n, the sum is at most 4n² + (2n−1)², which gives a quotient of at most about 2n − 1.
The printed text has 'quum' for 'quam' in §62 (typographical).

ideas.what: For p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and any a prime to p, there exists b with p | a² + b² and p ∤ a, b (from −1 being a quadratic residue).
ideas.modern_name: −1 is a quadratic residue mod p ≡ 1 (mod 4); first step of the two-squares theorem
ideas.where_published: E241 (Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani…), E262 and related papers; correspondence with Goldbach

ideas.what: Reduction of the partner x to the range 0 < x < p/2.
The involution a ↦ b on {1, …, (p−1)/2} has no fixed points, giving exactly (p−1)/4 distinct sums a² + b² ≡ 0 (mod p), each with quotient below about p/2.
ideas.modern_name: Pairing of solutions of a² + b² ≡ 0 mod p; small multiple m·p = a² + b² for descent
ideas.where_published: Likely implicit in E241; explicit counting of n pairs not commonly cited

deep.surprise_reason: Standard preparatory lemmas for Euler's well-known proof of the two-squares theorem. The explicit count of n pairs and the quotient bound are elementary and implicit in the known literature.
transcription_corrections: The image clearly shows 'quum' in §62; this is a printing error for 'quam', and the transcription correctly preserves it.
§61 opens 'Euidens quoque est quadratum xx infinitis modis…'; this is correct apart from the long-s forms.
